## Learning Outcomes {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## 🎯 Learning Outcomes

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Define** activities from a WBS and estimate their durations
2. **Sequence** activities using precedence relationships (FS, SS, FF, SF)
3. **Draw** a network diagram (AON) for a project
4. **Calculate** the Critical Path** using forward and backward pass
5. **Compute** total float and free float for all activities
6. **Develop** a Gantt chart from a network analysis
7. **Apply** PERT three-point estimation to handle uncertainty
8. **Explain** schedule compression techniques (crashing and fast-tracking)
:::

## Activity Definition and Duration Estimating

### From Work Packages to Activities

Work packages from the WBS must be further broken down into **schedule activities** — the individual tasks that can be tracked on a daily/weekly basis.

| WBS Work Package | Schedule Activities |
|-----------------|-------------------|
| 1.3.1 Foundation Design | A1: Geotechnical data review; A2: Foundation type analysis; A3: Structural calculations; A4: Foundation drawings; A5: Specification writing |
| 1.4.2 Concrete Structures | B1: Formwork fabrication; B2: Reinforcement fixing; B3: Concrete pouring; B4: Curing; B5: Formwork striking; B6: Surface finishing |

### Duration Estimation Methods

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Analogous Estimating
**Use historical data from similar projects**

- Fast and low effort
- Less accurate
- Best for early-stage estimates

*Example:* "Our last 50MW substation took 18 months, so this 60MW substation will take about 21 months"

Accuracy: ±25% to ±50%

## Parametric Estimating
**Use statistical relationships between variables**

- Uses unit rates or formulas
- More accurate than analogous
- Requires reliable data

*Example:* "Excavation rate for this soil type is 120m³/day with a 20-tonne excavator. We have 2,400m³ to excavate, so: 2,400 ÷ 120 = 20 days"

Accuracy: ±10% to ±25%

## Three-Point (PERT) Estimating
**Use optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates**

Three estimates for each activity:
- **Optimistic (O):** Best case, everything goes right
- **Most Likely (M):** Most realistic estimate
- **Pessimistic (P):** Worst case, everything goes wrong

**PERT Expected Duration:**
$$t_E = \frac{O + 4M + P}{6}$$

**PERT Standard Deviation:**
$$\sigma = \frac{P - O}{6}$$

**PERT Variance:**
$$\sigma^2 = \left(\frac{P - O}{6}\right)^2$$

## Bottom-Up Estimating
**Estimate each activity individually, then aggregate**

- Most accurate method
- Most time-consuming
- Best for detailed planning

*Process:*
1. Identify all activities
2. Estimate each individually with subject matter experts
3. Sum all activities for total project duration
4. Add buffer/contingency

Accuracy: ±5% to ±15%

:::

### Lag and Lead Time

- **Lag:** A delay after a dependency is satisfied
  - *Example:* Concrete curing — next activity starts 7 days after pouring finishes (FS + 7 days lag)
- **Lead:** An overlap — the successor activity starts before the predecessor finishes
  - *Example:* Begin procurement drawings while detailed design is still 80% complete (FS - 2 weeks lead)

## Network Diagrams — Activity on Node (AON)

The **Activity on Node (AON)** method represents activities as boxes (nodes) and dependencies as arrows:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Sample AON network diagram for a bridge design project"
graph LR
    START(["START"])
    A["A<br/>Site Survey<br/>5 days"]
    B["B<br/>Geotechnical<br/>Investigation<br/>10 days"]
    C["C<br/>Hydraulic<br/>Study<br/>7 days"]
    D["D<br/>Conceptual<br/>Design<br/>8 days"]
    E["E<br/>Foundation<br/>Design<br/>12 days"]
    F["F<br/>Structural<br/>Design<br/>15 days"]
    G["G<br/>Drainage<br/>Design<br/>6 days"]
    H["H<br/>Drawings<br/>Production<br/>10 days"]
    I["I<br/>Spec Writing<br/>5 days"]
    END(["END"])

    START --> A
    A --> B & C
    B --> D
    C --> D & G
    D --> E & F
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I
    I --> END

    style START fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff,stroke:#1d4ed8
    style END fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
```

## Critical Path Method (CPM)

The **Critical Path Method (CPM)** identifies the **longest path through the network** — the sequence of activities that determines the minimum project duration.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## 📖 CPM Basic Terms & Formulas

| Term | Formula | Meaning |
|------|---------|---------|
| **ES** — Early Start | $ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})$ | Earliest an activity can start |
| **EF** — Early Finish | $EF = ES + Duration$ | Earliest an activity can finish |
| **LF** — Late Finish | $LF = \min(LS \text{ of successors})$ | Latest it can finish without delaying the project |
| **LS** — Late Start | $LS = LF - Duration$ | Latest it can start without delaying the project |
| **Total Float** | $Float = LS - ES \;=\; LF - EF$ | Flexibility an activity has before it delays the project |
| **Free Float** | $FF = ES_{successor} - EF$ | Flexibility before delaying the *next* activity |
| **Critical Path** | Activities where $Float = 0$ | Longest path — determines total project duration |
| **Critical Activity** | $Float = 0$ | Any delay on this activity delays the entire project |
:::

### Step-by-Step CPM Calculation

**Example Network:**

| Activity | Duration (days) | Predecessors |
|----------|----------------|-------------|
| A | 3 | — |
| B | 5 | A |
| C | 4 | A |
| D | 6 | B |
| E | 3 | B, C |
| F | 4 | D, E |

**Step 1: Forward Pass (Calculate ES and EF)**

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## 💡 Starting Convention
The **first activity always has ES = 0** by convention — the project clock starts at zero. The formula $ES = \max(EF \text{ of predecessors})$ only applies to activities that have predecessors. Similarly, in the backward pass, **LF of the last activity = project duration** (not calculated from successors).
:::

$$ES_A = 0 \quad \text{(by convention — no predecessors)}, \quad EF_A = ES_A + Duration_A = 0 + 3 = 3$$

$$ES_B = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_B = 3 + 5 = 8$$

$$ES_C = EF_A = 3, \quad EF_C = 3 + 4 = 7$$

$$ES_D = EF_B = 8, \quad EF_D = 8 + 6 = 14$$

$$ES_E = \max(EF_B, EF_C) = \max(8, 7) = 8, \quad EF_E = 8 + 3 = 11$$

$$ES_F = \max(EF_D, EF_E) = \max(14, 11) = 14, \quad EF_F = 14 + 4 = 18$$

**Project Duration = 18 days**

**Step 2: Backward Pass (Calculate LS and LF)**

$$LF_F = 18 \quad \text{(by convention — equals project duration, no successors)}, \quad LS_F = LF_F - Duration_F = 18 - 4 = 14$$

$$LF_D = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_D = 14 - 6 = 8$$

$$LF_E = LS_F = 14, \quad LS_E = 14 - 3 = 11$$

$$LF_B = \min(LS_D, LS_E) = \min(8, 11) = 8, \quad LS_B = 8 - 5 = 3$$

$$LF_C = LS_E = 11, \quad LS_C = 11 - 4 = 7$$

$$LF_A = \min(LS_B, LS_C) = \min(3, 7) = 3, \quad LS_A = 3 - 3 = 0$$

**Step 3: Calculate Float**

$$Total\ Float = LS - ES = LF - EF$$

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 3 | 0 | 3 | **0** | ✅ YES |
| B | 3 | 8 | 3 | 8 | **0** | ✅ YES |
| C | 3 | 7 | 7 | 11 | **4** | NO |
| D | 8 | 14 | 8 | 14 | **0** | ✅ YES |
| E | 8 | 11 | 11 | 14 | **3** | NO |
| F | 14 | 18 | 14 | 18 | **0** | ✅ YES |

: CPM calculation results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: A → B → D → F (18 days)**

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Network with critical path highlighted"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 30, 'rankSpacing': 60}}}%%
graph LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"]) --> A
    A["A | Dur:3<br/>ES:0  EF:3 | Float:0"]
    B["B | Dur:5<br/>ES:3  EF:8 | Float:0"]
    C["C | Dur:4<br/>ES:3  EF:7 | Float:4"]
    D["D | Dur:6<br/>ES:8  EF:14 | Float:0"]
    E["E | Dur:3<br/>ES:8  EF:11 | Float:3"]
    F["F | Dur:4<br/>ES:14 EF:18 | Float:0"]
    FN(["End — Day 18"])

    A -->|"CRITICAL"| B
    A --> C
    B -->|"CRITICAL"| D
    B --> E
    C --> E
    D -->|"CRITICAL"| F
    E --> F
    S -->|"CRITICAL"| A
    F -->|"CRITICAL"| FN

    style A fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style B fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c

```

### More CPM Examples

Work through these five examples to master every dependency type and the parallel-start pattern.

### Example 1 — FS Network

**Four activities in a Finish-to-Start network with two parallel branches**

| Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Dependency |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------|
| A | 3 days | — | Start |
| B | 4 days | A | FS |
| C | 2 days | A | FS |
| D | 3 days | B, C | FS |

**Forward Pass**

$$ES_A = 0\;(\text{convention — no predecessors}),\quad EF_A = 0 + 3 = 3$$

$$ES_B = EF_A = 3,\quad EF_B = 3 + 4 = 7$$

$$ES_C = EF_A = 3,\quad EF_C = 3 + 2 = 5$$

$$ES_D = \max(EF_B,\,EF_C) = \max(7,\,5) = 7,\quad EF_D = 7 + 3 = 10$$

**Project Duration = 10 days**

**Backward Pass**

$$LF_D = 10\;(\text{convention — no successors}),\quad LS_D = 10 - 3 = 7$$

$$LF_B = LS_D = 7,\quad LS_B = 7 - 4 = 3$$

$$LF_C = LS_D = 7,\quad LS_C = 7 - 2 = 5$$

$$LF_A = \min(LS_B,\,LS_C) = \min(3,\,5) = 3,\quad LS_A = 3 - 3 = 0$$

**Float & Critical Path**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|-----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 3 | 0 | 3 | **0** | ✅ |
| B | 3 | 7 | 3 | 7 | **0** | ✅ |
| C | 3 | 5 | 5 | 7 | **2** | ❌ |
| D | 7 | 10 | 7 | 10 | **0** | ✅ |

: Ex 1 CPM results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: A → B → D (10 days)** — C has 2 days of float (can slip without delaying the project).

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55}}}%%
flowchart LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"])
    A["A | Dur:3<br/>ES:0  EF:3<br/>LS:0  LF:3 | F:0"]
    B["B | Dur:4<br/>ES:3  EF:7<br/>LS:3  LF:7 | F:0"]
    C["C | Dur:2<br/>ES:3  EF:5<br/>LS:5  LF:7 | F:2"]
    D["D | Dur:3<br/>ES:7  EF:10<br/>LS:7  LF:10 | F:0"]
    EN(["End — Day 10"])

    S -- CRITICAL --> A
    A -- CRITICAL --> B
    A --> C
    B -- CRITICAL --> D
    C --> D
    D -- CRITICAL --> EN

    style A fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style B fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style D fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style C fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#15803d,color:#fff
```

### Example 2 — SS + Lag

**Start-to-Start dependency: B can start 2 days after A starts (SS+2)**

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## 💡 SS Lag Rule
$$ES_B = ES_A + \text{lag}$$
In the backward pass: $LS_A = LS_B - \text{lag}$
Activities **overlap** in time — this is the whole point of SS.
:::

| Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Dependency |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------|
| A | 5 days | — | Start |
| B | 4 days | A | SS+2 |
| C | 3 days | B | FS |

**Forward Pass**

$$ES_A = 0\;(\text{convention}),\quad EF_A = 0 + 5 = 5$$

$$ES_B = ES_A + \text{lag} = 0 + 2 = 2,\quad EF_B = 2 + 4 = 6$$

*Note: A runs from day 0–5; B starts at day 2 while A is still in progress (overlap intended).*

$$ES_C = EF_B = 6,\quad EF_C = 6 + 3 = 9$$

**Project Duration = 9 days**

**Backward Pass**

$$LF_C = 9\;(\text{convention}),\quad LS_C = 9 - 3 = 6$$

$$LF_B = LS_C = 6,\quad LS_B = 6 - 4 = 2$$

$$LS_A = LS_B - \text{lag} = 2 - 2 = 0,\quad LF_A = LS_A + Dur_A = 0 + 5 = 5$$

*The SS+2 backward rule forces A to start no later than day 0.*

**Float & Critical Path**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|-----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 5 | 0 | 5 | **0** | ✅ |
| B | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | **0** | ✅ |
| C | 6 | 9 | 6 | 9 | **0** | ✅ |

: Ex 2 CPM results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: A → B → C (9 days)** — All activities are critical; no float anywhere.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55}}}%%
flowchart LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"])
    A["A | Dur:5\nES:0  EF:5\nLS:0  LF:5 | F:0"]
    B["B | Dur:4\nES:2  EF:6\nLS:2  LF:6 | F:0"]
    C["C | Dur:3\nES:6  EF:9\nLS:6  LF:9 | F:0"]
    EN(["End — Day 9"])

    S -- CRITICAL --> A
    A -- SS+2 lag --> B
    B -- CRITICAL --> C
    C -- CRITICAL --> EN

    style A fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style B fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style C fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#15803d,color:#fff
```

### Example 3 — FF Dependency

**Finish-to-Finish dependency: B cannot finish until A finishes (FF+0)**

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## 💡 FF Lag Rule
$$ES_B = \max\!\bigl(0,\; EF_A + \text{lag} - Dur_B\bigr)$$
$$EF_B = ES_B + Dur_B \;\geq\; EF_A + \text{lag}$$
In the backward pass: $LF_A = LF_B - \text{lag}$
:::

| Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Dependency |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------|
| A | 6 days | — | Start |
| B | 4 days | A | FF+0 |
| C | 2 days | B | FS |

**Forward Pass**

$$ES_A = 0\;(\text{convention}),\quad EF_A = 0 + 6 = 6$$

$$ES_B = \max(0,\;EF_A + 0 - Dur_B) = \max(0,\;6 - 4) = 2,\quad EF_B = 2 + 4 = 6$$

*B must finish no earlier than A (day 6), so B is pushed to start at day 2.*

$$ES_C = EF_B = 6,\quad EF_C = 6 + 2 = 8$$

**Project Duration = 8 days**

**Backward Pass**

$$LF_C = 8\;(\text{convention}),\quad LS_C = 8 - 2 = 6$$

$$LF_B = LS_C = 6,\quad LS_B = 6 - 4 = 2$$

$$LF_A = LF_B - \text{lag} = 6 - 0 = 6,\quad LS_A = 6 - 6 = 0$$

**Float & Critical Path**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|-----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 6 | 0 | 6 | **0** | ✅ |
| B | 2 | 6 | 2 | 6 | **0** | ✅ |
| C | 6 | 8 | 6 | 8 | **0** | ✅ |

: Ex 3 CPM results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: A → B → C (8 days)** — B cannot finish before A, pulling the entire chain tight.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55}}}%%
flowchart LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"])
    A["A | Dur:6<br/>ES:0  EF:6<br/>LS:0  LF:6 | F:0"]
    B["B | Dur:4<br/>ES:2  EF:6<br/>LS:2  LF:6 | F:0"]
    C["C | Dur:2<br/>ES:6  EF:8<br/>LS:6  LF:8 | F:0"]
    EN(["End — Day 8"])

    S -- CRITICAL --> A
    A -- FF+0 --> B
    B -- CRITICAL --> C
    C -- CRITICAL --> EN

    style A fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style B fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style C fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#15803d,color:#fff
```

### Example 4 — SF Dependency

**Start-to-Finish (rare): B cannot finish until A starts (+1 day lag)**

::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
## ⚠️ SF is the Rarest Dependency
The predecessor (A) **starts** before the successor (B) can **finish**.
Classic use case: an old system (B) must keep running until the new system (A) goes live.
$$EF_B \;\geq\; ES_A + \text{lag}$$
In the backward pass: $LS_A \leq LF_B - \text{lag}$
:::

| Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Dependency |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------|
| A | 3 days | — | Start |
| B | 5 days | A | SF+1 |

**Forward Pass**

$$ES_A = 0\;(\text{convention}),\quad EF_A = 0 + 3 = 3$$

B has no start constraint from the SF link (SF only constrains B's *finish*):

$$ES_B = 0\;(\text{no start constraint}),\quad EF_B = 0 + 5 = 5$$

Check SF+1 constraint: $EF_B = 5 \geq ES_A + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1\;\checkmark$

**Project Duration = max(EF_A, EF_B) = max(3, 5) = 5 days**

**Backward Pass**

Neither A nor B has FS successors, so both LFs are set to the project duration:

$$LF_B = 5\;(\text{project end}),\quad LS_B = 5 - 5 = 0$$

SF+1 backward constraint: $LS_A \leq LF_B - \text{lag} = 5 - 1 = 4$

$$LF_A = 5\;(\text{project end}),\quad LS_A = 5 - 3 = 2$$

Check: $LS_A = 2 \leq 4\;\checkmark$ (SF constraint not the binding factor — B's own duration drives the schedule)

**Float & Critical Path**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|-----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 3 | 2 | 5 | **2** | ❌ |
| B | 0 | 5 | 0 | 5 | **0** | ✅ |

: Ex 4 CPM results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: B (5 days)** — A has 2 days of float. B's long duration dominates; the SF constraint is satisfied without binding the schedule.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55}}}%%
flowchart LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"])
    A["A | Dur:3<br/>ES:0  EF:3<br/>LS:2  LF:5 | F:2"]
    B["B | Dur:5<br/>ES:0  EF:5<br/>LS:0  LF:5 | F:0"]
    EN(["End — Day 5"])

    S --> A
    S -- CRITICAL --> B
    A -- SF+1 lag --> B
    B -- CRITICAL --> EN
    A --> EN

    style A fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style B fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#15803d,color:#fff
```

### Example 5 — Parallel Starts

**Two activities with no predecessors both start on Day 0, creating parallel chains**

| Activity | Duration | Predecessor | Dependency |
|----------|----------|-------------|------------|
| A | 4 days | — | Start |
| B | 3 days | — | Start |
| C | 5 days | A | FS |
| D | 2 days | B | FS |
| E | 3 days | C, D | FS |

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## 💡 Multiple Starting Activities
When two or more activities have **no predecessors**, they all receive $ES = 0$ by convention. They run in parallel from day 0.
:::

**Forward Pass**

$$ES_A = 0\;(\text{convention}),\quad EF_A = 0 + 4 = 4$$

$$ES_B = 0\;(\text{convention}),\quad EF_B = 0 + 3 = 3$$

$$ES_C = EF_A = 4,\quad EF_C = 4 + 5 = 9$$

$$ES_D = EF_B = 3,\quad EF_D = 3 + 2 = 5$$

$$ES_E = \max(EF_C,\,EF_D) = \max(9,\,5) = 9,\quad EF_E = 9 + 3 = 12$$

**Project Duration = 12 days**

**Backward Pass**

$$LF_E = 12\;(\text{convention}),\quad LS_E = 12 - 3 = 9$$

$$LF_C = LS_E = 9,\quad LS_C = 9 - 5 = 4$$

$$LF_D = LS_E = 9,\quad LS_D = 9 - 2 = 7$$

$$LF_A = LS_C = 4,\quad LS_A = 4 - 4 = 0$$

$$LF_B = LS_D = 9,\quad LS_B = 9 - 3 = 6$$

**Float & Critical Path**

| Activity | ES | EF | LS | LF | Float | Critical? |
|----------|----|----|----|-----|-------|-----------|
| A | 0 | 4 | 0 | 4 | **0** | ✅ |
| B | 0 | 3 | 6 | 9 | **6** | ❌ |
| C | 4 | 9 | 4 | 9 | **0** | ✅ |
| D | 3 | 5 | 7 | 9 | **4** | ❌ |
| E | 9 | 12 | 9 | 12 | **0** | ✅ |

: Ex 5 CPM results {.striped .hover}

**Critical Path: A → C → E (12 days)** — Chain B→D is non-critical; B has 6 days float, D has 4 days float.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'nodeSpacing': 25, 'rankSpacing': 55}}}%%
flowchart LR
    S(["Start — Day 0"])
    A["A | Dur:4<br/>ES:0  EF:4<br/>LS:0  LF:4 | F:0"]
    B["B | Dur:3<br/>ES:0  EF:3<br/>LS:6  LF:9 | F:6"]
    C["C | Dur:5<br/>ES:4  EF:9<br/>LS:4  LF:9 | F:0"]
    D["D | Dur:2<br/>ES:3  EF:5<br/>LS:7  LF:9 | F:4"]
    E["E | Dur:3<br/>ES:9  EF:12<br/>LS:9  LF:12 | F:0"]
    EN(["End — Day 12"])

    S -- CRITICAL --> A
    S --> B
    A -- CRITICAL --> C
    B --> D
    C -- CRITICAL --> E
    D --> E
    E -- CRITICAL --> EN

    style A fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style C fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style E fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff,stroke:#b91c1c
    style B fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style D fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#22c55e,color:#166534
    style S fill:#1d4ed8,color:#fff
    style EN fill:#15803d,color:#fff
```

## Gantt Charts

A **Gantt Chart** is a bar chart that visually represents the project schedule against a timeline.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Gantt chart for a bridge construction project"
gantt
    title Bridge Construction Project Schedule
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat  %b %d
    
    section Investigations
    Site Survey              :done,    survey,   2026-01-05, 5d
    Geotechnical Drilling    :done,    geotech,  2026-01-12, 15d
    Hydraulic Study          :active,  hydro,    2026-01-12, 10d
    
    section Design
    Concept Design           :         concept,  after geotech, 10d
    Foundation Design        :         found,    after concept, 14d
    Structural Design        :crit,    struct,   after concept, 20d
    Drainage Design          :         drain,    after hydro, 8d
    Design Documentation     :crit,    docs,     after struct, 12d
    
    section Approvals
    Client Review            :crit,    review,   after docs, 7d
    Regulatory Approval      :         reg,      after docs, 21d
    
    section Construction
    Mobilisation             :crit,    mob,      after review, 5d
    Abutment Excavation      :crit,    excav,    after mob, 15d
    Abutment Concrete        :crit,    conc,     after excav, 20d
    Steel Fabrication        :         steel_fab, after struct, 35d
    Steel Erection           :crit,    erect,    after conc, 10d
    Deck Construction        :crit,    deck,     after erect, 14d
    Handrail & Finishes      :         finish,   after deck, 10d
    
    section Commissioning
    Load Testing             :crit,    test,     after deck, 5d
    Handover                 :milestone, handover, after test, 0d
```

### Gantt Chart Best Practices

::: {.panel-tabset}

## What to Include
- All Level 3-4 WBS activities
- Milestones at key decision points
- Critical path activities (highlighted in red or marked as critical)
- Dependencies shown as arrows (where tools allow)
- Resource allocations (who is responsible for each bar)
- Planned vs. Actual tracking capability
- Baseline vs. Current schedule view

## Milestones
**Milestones** are zero-duration events marking significant project achievements:

Common engineering project milestones:
- ✓ Project Kick-off
- ✓ Investigations Complete
- ✓ 30% Design Issue for Review
- ✓ 60% Design Issue for Review
- ✓ 100% Design Issue for Construction
- ✓ Regulatory Approval Received
- ✓ Construction Start
- ✓ Structural Works Complete
- ✓ Commissioning Complete
- ✓ Practical Completion
- ✓ Defects Liability Period End

## Baseline vs. Current
A well-managed Gantt chart always shows:

1. **Baseline** (original approved schedule) — shown as the lower bar or grey shadow
2. **Current** (updated actual progress) — shown as the main coloured bar
3. **% Complete** — progress indicator on each bar

*If Current = Baseline, the project is on track.*  
*If Current extends beyond Baseline, analysis is needed.*

:::

---

## PERT Analysis — Handling Schedule Uncertainty

**PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique)** extends CPM by acknowledging that activity durations are **uncertain** and modelling them probabilistically.

### PERT Three-Point Estimating

For each activity, obtain three estimates:

| Activity | Optimistic (O) | Most Likely (M) | Pessimistic (P) | Expected ($t_E$) | Std Dev ($\sigma$) | Variance |
|----------|---------|---------|----------|---------|--------|---------|
| Foundation Design | 8 | 12 | 22 | **12.67** | **2.33** | 5.44 |
| Structural Design | 12 | 18 | 30 | **18.67** | **3.00** | 9.00 |
| Drawing Production | 6 | 9 | 15 | **9.17** | **1.50** | 2.25 |
| Approvals | 14 | 21 | 56 | **23.33** | **7.00** | 49.00 |

**Project Expected Duration** = Sum of expected durations on critical path

**Project Standard Deviation**: 
$$\sigma_{project} = \sqrt{\sum \sigma^2_{critical\ activities}}$$

### Probability of Completion by Target Date

Using the normal distribution:

$$Z = \frac{T_{target} - T_{expected}}{\sigma_{project}}$$

Where $T_{target}$ is the desired completion date and $T_{expected}$ is the calculated expected completion.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## 📖 Example PERT Probability Calculation

**Critical path expected duration:** 65 days  
**Project standard deviation:** 8.5 days  
**Client deadline:** 75 days  

$$Z = \frac{75 - 65}{8.5} = 1.18$$

From Z-table: P(Z ≤ 1.18) ≈ **88%**

There is an **88% probability** of completing the project within 75 days.

To achieve 95% probability: Need Z = 1.645 → $T = 65 + (1.645 × 8.5) = 79$ days
:::

---

## Schedule Compression Techniques

When the calculated schedule exceeds the target date, two primary compression techniques are available:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Schedule compression strategies — crashing vs. fast-tracking"
graph LR
    SC["📅 Schedule<br/>Needs<br/>Compression"] --> CR & FT
    
    subgraph CR["💰 CRASHING"]
        direction TB
        CR1["Add more resources to<br/>critical path activities"] --> CR2
        CR2["Increases cost,<br/>may increase risk<br/>but maintains quality"] --> CR3
        CR3["Cost-slope analysis:<br/>Which activity gives<br/>most time per $?"]
    end
    
    subgraph FT["⚠️ FAST-TRACKING"]
        direction TB
        FT1["Run activities in<br/>parallel that were<br/>previously sequential"] --> FT2
        FT2["Increases risk<br/>(rework if earlier<br/>work changes)"] --> FT3
        FT3["No additional cost<br/>but needs careful<br/>coordination"]
    end

    style SC fill:#b91c1c,color:#fff
    style CR fill:#fef9c3,stroke:#eab308
    style FT fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#ef4444
```

### Cost-Slope for Crashing

The **cost-slope** tells you how much it costs to shorten an activity by one unit of time:

$$Cost\ Slope = \frac{Crash\ Cost - Normal\ Cost}{Normal\ Duration - Crash\ Duration}$$

**Crashing priority:** Always crash the critical path activity with the **lowest cost-slope** first, then re-analyse.

| Activity | Normal Duration | Crash Duration | Normal Cost | Crash Cost | Cost Slope |
|----------|----------------|----------------|-------------|------------|------------|
| A | 10 days | 7 days | $10,000 | $16,000 | **$2,000/day** |
| B | 8 days | 6 days | $8,000 | $12,000 | **$2,000/day** |
| C | 15 days | 11 days | $20,000 | $32,000 | **$3,000/day** |
| D | 12 days | 9 days | $15,000 | $24,000 | **$3,000/day** |

*To save 2 days: Crash Activity A or B first ($4,000 total), not C or D ($6,000 total)*

## Case Study — Qatar FIFA World Cup 2022: Scheduling the Unschedulable {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## 🏭 Case Study: Qatar 2022 — When the Deadline Cannot Move

**Background:**  
On 21 November 2022, the FIFA World Cup opened at Al-Bayt Stadium in Al-Khor, Qatar — the first World Cup hosted by an Arab nation. For Qatar's Supreme Committee for Delivery & Legacy (SC), the scheduling challenge was unique: the tournament date was set in December 2010 and could not shift by even a single day. This created a project scheduling environment where float on the critical path was, ultimately, zero.

**The Scale:**
- **8 world-class stadiums** built or substantially reconstructed (most World Cup hosts refurbish existing facilities)
- **Hard deadline:** 21 November 2022 — fixed 12 years in advance
- **Construction workforce:** 30,000+ workers across stadium sites simultaneously
- **Largest stadium:** Lusail Stadium (88,966 capacity) — the centrepiece venue for the final

**Scheduling Challenges:**

| Challenge | Response |
|-----------|----------|
| Summer temperatures reaching 50°C made daytime work impossible June–September | Shifted all critical construction to **mandatory night shifts** (22:00–06:00); stadium cooling systems tested 18 months early to enable summer commissioning |
| COVID-19 pandemic (March 2020) halted construction for 4–6 weeks | Critical path reassessed immediately; non-critical works suspended; critical path workers resumed in isolated bubbles within 3 weeks |
| Lusail Stadium — largest design, started last | Assigned highest resource density of any stadium; 24-hour operations from 2018; Lusail became first stadium to complete trial events in 2021 despite being the last to start |
| Al-Thumama Stadium required partial structural redesign mid-construction | Design frozen at 60% completion; structural changes fast-tracked through review cycles; construction sequence reordered around the redesigned elements |
| All 8 stadiums required fully operational cooling systems *before* commissioning began | MEP commissioning placed on the critical path from contract start — 3 months bought back by accelerating installation sequence |

**CPM Application:**  
The SC's scheduling team used **Oracle Primavera P6 Enterprise** with a master programme of **35,000+ activities**. The critical path ran through Lusail Stadium's seating bowl and roof structure — the most complex and the last to mobilise. Any activity reaching **< 5 days of total float** triggered an automatic Managing Director-level review within 24 hours.

**The Fixed Deadline Strategy:**
1. Each stadium committed to completion **6 months before the tournament** — allowing full test event cycles
2. Three rounds of test events per stadium: Fan Experience Tests, Operational Readiness Tests, and FIFA Final Certification
3. A parallel **maximum acceleration schedule** was pre-approved and ready to activate — with pre-agreed resource profiles and contractor incentive payments — if the primary programme was ever threatened

**Outcome:**  
All 8 stadiums were delivered on or before their committed test event dates. The tournament opened on its announced date. Qatar Stadium 974 — a temporary venue built from shipping containers — was delivered as a surprise late addition and met its commissioning deadline.

**Key Scheduling Lessons:**
1. When the deadline is absolute, schedule contingency must be proportionally large — planning to finish "just in time" is planning to fail
2. External disruptions (COVID, extreme heat) will invalidate sections of any schedule — the organisations that survived maintained pre-developed recovery plans
3. Risk-driven sequencing: the most complex activities (Lusail's roof) were started earliest and given the most resources
4. Automatic escalation triggers on critical float are more reliable than human judgment — at 5 days of float with 30,000 workers in play, human review is too slow

*Sources: @fifaqatar2022; @sc2023legacy*
:::

## ✏️ Exercise 4.1 — Activity Sequencing

For the following activities in a **pump station construction project**, determine the logical dependencies and draw an AON network diagram:

| Activity | Description | Duration |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| A | Site survey and clearance | 5 days |
| B | Excavation | 8 days |
| C | Dewatering system installation | 3 days |
| D | Base slab concrete | 5 days |
| E | Wall concrete (lift 1) | 4 days |
| F | Wall concrete (lift 2) | 4 days |
| G | Mechanical equipment delivery | 15 days |
| H | Equipment installation | 6 days |
| I | Pipework installation | 8 days |
| J | Electrical installation | 7 days |
| K | Testing and commissioning | 5 days |

**Note:** B requires A; C requires B; D requires B, C; E requires D with 7-day lag (curing); F requires E with 7-day lag; G can start immediately (long lead item); H requires F and G; I requires H; J requires H; K requires I and J.

1. Draw the network diagram
2. Perform forward and backward pass
3. Identify the critical path
4. Calculate total float for all activities
:::

|----------|---------|-------------|
| A | 4 | — |
| B | 6 | A |
| C | 3 | A |
| D | 8 | B |
| E | 5 | B, C |
| F | 4 | C |
| G | 7 | D, E |
| H | 3 | E, F |
| I | 6 | G, H |
| J | 2 | I |

1. Draw the network diagram
2. Calculate ES, EF, LS, LF, and Total Float for every activity

## ✏️ Exercise 4.3 — PERT Analysis

An engineering firm is designing a new water reservoir. The critical path activities have the following three-point estimates:

| Activity | Optimistic | Most Likely | Pessimistic |
|----------|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| 1: Feasibility | 3 weeks | 5 weeks | 9 weeks |
| 2: Site Investigation | 4 weeks | 6 weeks | 14 weeks |
| 3: Concept Design | 5 weeks | 8 weeks | 11 weeks |
| 4: Detailed Design | 10 weeks | 14 weeks | 24 weeks |
| 5: Approvals | 8 weeks | 12 weeks | 28 weeks |

1. Calculate the expected duration and standard deviation for each activity
2. Calculate the total expected project duration and overall standard deviation

## ✏️ Exercise 4.4 — Schedule Crashing

Your project has a critical path of 30 days, but the contract requires delivery in 26 days. You need to crash 4 days off the schedule.

| Activity | Normal Duration | Crash Duration | Normal Cost | Crash Cost | On Critical Path? |
|----------|----------------|----------------|-------------|------------|----------|
| A | 8 | 5 | $12,000 | $18,000 | Yes |
| B | 10 | 7 | $25,000 | $34,000 | Yes |
| C | 6 | 4 | $8,000 | $14,000 | Yes |
| D | 6 | 5 | $10,000 | $13,000 | Yes |
| E | 7 | 5 | $9,000 | $15,000 | No (Float = 3) |

1. Calculate the cost-slope for each activity
2. Select the activities to crash and in what order
3. What is the minimum additional cost to achieve the 26-day schedule?
4. Draw a **time-cost trade-off curve** for this project (cost vs. project duration from 30 to 26 days)
5. Should you also consider fast-tracking? Which activities could be overlapped?

## 🖥️ MS Project Practice — Scheduling {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Microsoft Project: Applying Chapter 4 Concepts

Now that you understand activity sequencing, CPM, and Gantt charts, apply these directly in MS Project using the AAUP Wi-Fi Upgrade case study (Chapter 6) or your own project:

**Tasks to complete in MS Project:**

1. **Enter the activity list** from your WBS as auto-scheduled tasks with correct indentation (summary tasks → sub-tasks)
2. **Set durations** using the estimates from your Activity List (type `5d`, `2w`, etc.)
3. **Enter predecessors** for each task — use FS, SS, FF with any lags (e.g., `3SS+1d`)
4. **View the Network Diagram** (View → Network Diagram): verify that the logic matches your hand-drawn AON diagram
5. **View the Critical Path**: Format tab → check "Critical Tasks" — all red tasks form the critical path
6. **Check Total Float**: Add the Total Slack column (right-click any column header → Insert Column → Total Slack). Zero = critical.
7. **Simulate a delay**: Add a 3-day lag to one critical task — observe how MS Project recalculates the finish date automatically
8. **Apply schedule compression**: Try reducing the duration of a critical task (crashing) and observe the new project finish date

**Expected outcome:** Your MS Project schedule should match the CPM calculations you did by hand. If they differ, check for missing dependencies or manual scheduling overrides.
:::
